title: The Feature Factory: Why Shipping More Features Doesn't Mean You're Winning
excerpt: The most dangerous trap in product management isn't failure — it's building features that work perfectly and change nothing. Here's how to escape the output mindset.
content:
There's a pattern I see at company after company: the product team is shipping faster than ever. Two-week sprints, daily standups, velocity charts trending upward. The roadmap is full. The backlog is groomed. And yet, quarter after quarter, the business metrics barely move.

This is the feature factory — an organization that has confused output with outcome, activity with impact. It's not a failure of execution. It's a failure of framing.

The Factory Mentality

The feature factory doesn't announce itself. It creeps in through well-intentioned practices: OKRs measured in features shipped, roadmaps committed six months in advance, success defined as "on time, on budget." Before long, the team's identity becomes tied to delivery itself — not to what that delivery changes.

The telltale signs are everywhere:

  • Velocity is the primary metric. Teams celebrate story points completed, not problems solved.
  • The roadmap is a commitment, not a hypothesis. Features are "promised" to stakeholders, not "proposed" as experiments.
  • Success means launch. No one measures what happens after the feature goes live.
  • Discovery is a phase, not a practice. Research happens before the roadmap is set, then the team switches to execution mode.

The factory feels productive. It looks productive. It is, in the most literal sense, producing — just not value.

Why Smart PMs Fall Into It

The feature factory isn't staffed by bad people. It's staffed by people responding to the incentives they're given. When a PM's performance review depends on "features delivered," they will deliver features — even if those features don't move the needle.

There's also a psychological comfort in the factory. Shipping features is tangible. You can point at a release and say "I did that." Outcomes are messy — they're influenced by timing, market conditions, and factors outside your control. It's easier to measure what you can control (output) than to own what you can't fully control (outcome).

But ease of measurement is not the same as importance of measurement.

The Outcome Shift

Escaping the feature factory requires a fundamental reframe: you are not in the business of building features. You are in the business of changing behavior.

A feature is a means. The behavior change is the end. A checkout redesign isn't successful because it shipped — it's successful because it increased completion rates. A notification system isn't valuable because it exists — it's valuable because it brought back users who would have churned.

This shift changes everything about how you work:

1. Start with the behavior, not the solution

Before you write a spec, articulate the specific behavior you want to change. "Users should share more" is vague. "Users who complete onboarding should invite at least one teammate within 7 days" is specific. The first leads to a feature brainstorm. The second leads to a testable hypothesis.

2. Define success before you build

For every initiative, write down: "We'll know this worked if we see [specific metric change] by [specific date]." If you can't fill in that sentence, you're not ready to build. You're guessing.

3. Measure what happens after launch

The two weeks after a feature ships are more important than the two months before. Did the behavior change? Did the metric move? If not, the feature didn't work — no matter how well it was built.

4. Kill features that don't earn their keep

Every feature has a maintenance cost. Every feature competes for attention in your UI. If a feature isn't driving the behavior it was designed for, remove it. The bravest thing a PM can do is sunset something they shipped.

The Roadmap as a Set of Hypotheses

In a feature factory, the roadmap is a plan. In an outcome-driven team, the roadmap is a set of bets. Each initiative should be framed as: "We believe that [doing this] will [change this behavior], which will [move this metric]."

This framing does something powerful: it makes disagreement productive. When the roadmap is a plan, challenging a feature feels like challenging the PM's competence. When the roadmap is a hypothesis, challenging the feature is just good scientific practice.

The Hard Truth

Most features don't work. Not because they're badly built, but because they're based on untested assumptions about what users need. The feature factory hides this truth behind a wall of shipping activity. An outcome-driven team confronts it early and often.

The goal isn't to ship less. It's to ship with intention — to build only the features that change the behaviors that drive the metrics that matter. Everything else is just noise.

Stop measuring how much you're building. Start measuring what it changes.
